In mathematics, specifically in [[order theory]] and [[functional analysis]], a subset <math>S</math> of a [[vector lattice]] <math>X</math> is said to be '''solid''' and is called an '''ideal''' if for all <math>s \in S</math> and <math>x \in X,</math> if <math>|x| \leq |s|</math> then <math>x \in S.</math> 
An [[ordered vector space]] whose order is Archimedean is said to be ''[[Archimedean order]]ed''.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204–214}} 
If <math>S\subseteq X</math> then the '''ideal generated by <math>S</math>''' is the smallest ideal in <math>X</math> containing <math>S.</math> 
An ideal generated by a singleton set is called a '''principal ideal''' in <math>X.</math> 

== Examples ==
The intersection of an arbitrary collection of ideals in <math>X</math> is again an ideal and furthermore, <math>X</math> is clearly an ideal of itself. 
thus every subset of <math>X</math> is contained in a unique smallest ideal.

In a [[locally convex vector lattice]] <math>X,</math> the [[polar set|polar]] of every solid neighborhood of the origin is a solid subset of the continuous dual space <math>X^{\prime}</math>; 
moreover, the family of all solid equicontinuous subsets of <math>X^{\prime}</math> is a fundamental family of equicontinuous sets, the polars (in bidual <math>X^{\prime\prime}</math>) form a neighborhood base of the origin for the natural topology on <math>X^{\prime\prime}</math> (that is, the topology of uniform convergence on equicontinuous subsets of <math>X^{\prime}</math>).{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=234–242}}

== Properties ==

* A solid subspace of a vector lattice <math>X</math> is necessarily a sublattice of <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204–214}} 
* If <math>N</math> is a solid subspace of a vector lattice <math>X</math> then the quotient <math>X/N</math> is a vector lattice (under the canonical order).{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204–214}}
